scenes.title:
Old spacecraft.
A new way in.
scenes.body:
A mobile companion for amateur radio
and satellite hobbyists.
subs: zombieSatellite brings forgotten spacecraft into a hands-on mobile experience.
Find the next pass, point your phone, and follow the computed Doppler shift.

scenes.title:
Seven satellites.
Documented history.
scenes.body:
Explore the people and discoveries
behind the zombie satellites.
scenes.note: Historical receptions are not app activity.
subs: The archive connects each spacecraft to its documented history.
IMAGE was rediscovered in 2018 by radio amateur Scott Tilley.

scenes.title:
Put the orbit
in your view.
scenes.body:
Use the phone camera as a backdrop
for the computed satellite direction.
scenes.note: This recording shows the app on a phone.
subs: The AR view places the calculated satellite direction over the phone camera.
Switch satellites to explore their different positions in the sky.

scenes.title:
See where
to look.
scenes.body:
Sky view, direction cues and orbit arcs
help you orient the phone.
scenes.note: Below-horizon objects are labelled in the app.
subs: The sky view keeps the orbit geometry visible without the camera backdrop.
Direction cues help you find an object even when it is outside the view.

scenes.title:
Know when
to begin.
scenes.body:
Choose a spacecraft and inspect
its next pass over your location.
scenes.note: Pass times are shown in UTC.
subs: Pass predictions use public orbital data and the observer location.
Choose a satellite, open its session, and start the 60x demo.

scenes.title:
A whole pass.
At 60x speed.
scenes.body:
Practise the session with auto-point
before trying it in real time.
scenes.note: Accelerated simulation of a predicted pass.
subs: This is demo mode with auto-point: a predicted pass played at 60x speed.

scenes.title:
Watch the
Doppler shift.
scenes.body:
The displayed kHz value follows
the computed orbital motion.
subs: Follow the pointing lock and watch the Doppler readout change through the pass.
The beacon tone is simulated. The phone receives no satellite radio signal.

scenes.title:
Finish the pass.
Review the result.
scenes.body:
See locked time, lock ratio
and best pointing error.
scenes.note: Results here come from demo mode.
subs: At the end of the pass, review the session and open your QSL collection.

scenes.title:
Keep a record
of the experience.
scenes.body:
QSL cards record the satellite,
timing and session details.
scenes.note: Cards explicitly distinguish simulation from RF.
subs: Each completed session produces a QSL card in the amateur radio tradition.
The cards are labelled as simulated sessions, not proof of real reception.

scenes.title:
Spec by spec.
Then into code.
scenes.body:
Feature requirements, design and tasks
are kept alongside the implementation.
subs: Kiro development is documented in eleven feature specs and two steering files.
The specs cover orbit prediction, pointing, sessions, QSL cards and the app shell.

scenes.title:
The orbit is real.
The beacon
is simulated.
scenes.body:
Try a pass on your phone.
Bring your own radio for real listening.
subs: Try zombieSatellite: find a pass, point your phone, and follow the orbit.
